I have spent about fifteen years now watching senior people work a room, and I do something at those events that sounds strange when I say it out loud. I count. I stand near two people who are talking, and I count how many questions each of them asks. The number is almost never equal. One of them asks eight questions in ten minutes and the other asks none, and when they walk away, I already know which one will get the follow-up email. It has nothing to do with charm and nothing to do with language. The person who asked is the one who will be remembered, because a week later nobody remembers what the other person said. They remember how they felt while they were saying it, and people feel good when someone is genuinely interested in them. So here is the part that senior people resist the most. You do not have to be interesting. That is a huge relief, and almost nobody believes me the first time. You have to be interested, which is a completely different job and a much easier one. And when you run out of things to say, which happens to everybody, do not change the subject and do not reach for a new topic. Go back to the last thing the other person said and ask about it in three words. How so. Such as. Since when. That is the entire technique. It fits on the back of a business card, and I have watched it change careers.

Note to myself before I forget the details of this afternoon. Final round with the infrastructure candidate, one hour, and I want to be very clear about why I am hesitating, because it is not the obvious thing. The answers were strong. Clear, well structured, real numbers in them, and when I pushed on the failed program he did not get defensive, which is rare. On paper this is a yes. But something was off for the whole hour and it took me until the parking lot to name it. He never asked me anything. Not one question, not about the team, not about the roadmap, not about why the role is open, not even about me. So the hour felt like a test he was passing rather than a conversation between two people who might work together on Monday. And that matters here, because the job is eighty percent talking to people who do not report to him. If he cannot get curious with the person deciding whether to hire him, I do not know what he does in a room with a vendor. So two things. Keep him in the process, I am not saying no. And when you brief the next ones, tell them from me to bring two or three real questions and to ask them early, in the middle of the conversation, not saved up for the last four minutes when everybody is already looking at the clock.

First I open with something light about the place or the trip. Then I listen for one thing we have in common. When he tells me something, I echo it with the auxiliary he used. After that I ask one short follow-up question and let him talk. And before I leave, I say I will touch base, and I write his name down.
